items.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003
items.q: And the Montgomery brothers, Wes, Buddy and Monk were there. And Monk befriended me

ctx.x: He never would have reached a hundred.

My uncle didn’t tell me that, Eubie told me that, which is great. So playing music and then as I was a kid I was a part of a music club and all the young musicians around town like Freddie Hubbard, Virgil Jones, Mel Ryan and David Hardiman, on and on, we all came up playing jazz. And the Montgomery brothers, Wes, Buddy and Monk were there. And Monk befriended me, and it’s very interesting how as a young teenager — well first, how I came to play the bass was I went to a Jazz at the Philharmonic concert. And Ray…

items.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003
items.q: He said, “Look kid, I’m going out to the west coast... and I want you to fill in for me.” ... That was his way of teaching me. He never really gave me a lesson other than me absorbing and listening and watching and listening to him perform.

ctx.x: I’m sorry, I missed what you said.

The group with Freddie Hubbard and Jimmy Spaulding and first Walt Miller then Al Plank and Paul Parker was the drummer. And then we used to play with Wes. The first time I saw Monk Montgomery and I approached him about taking lessons from him he told me, “Well come over to the house, kid.” I went over to the house and there is Wes sitting up there with the guitar and his brother Buddy at the piano. A saxophone player by the name of Pookie Johnson and the drummer Sonny Johnson. They called themselves the…

having good ears. You know because when you’re up there improvising you’re not thinking about oh I’m going from a D minor seventh with a flat five over here to a G seven with a raised nine. You’re not thinking about all that. You’ve got to sit at the piano and you’ve got to get that sound, or the guitar, and get those sounds in your ear and know how to respond to that improvisationally through hearing lyrical lines. And that’s one of the things I’m concerned about that is happening with jazz education. Too many…
